title: One message through MimiClaw — step-by-step
example_input: turn on the relay on pin 5
note: Representations below are simplified shapes of the real types at the pinned SHA, not verbatim dumps.

steps.title: Telegram update arrives
steps.narrative: The Telegram poll task's long-polling getUpdates returns an update with the text 'turn on the relay on pin 5'. process_updates checks the update against the NVS-persisted offset and the seen-message dedup ring, then wraps it in a mimi_msg_t — channel 'telegram', the chat id, and a heap copy of the text — and pushes it to the inbound queue. The bot applies no sender check: any chat that messages it reaches this point.

steps.title: Message waits on the bus
steps.narrative: The inbound queue is a FreeRTOS queue of depth 16 holding mimi_msg_t values; ownership of the content pointer transfers with the push. If the queue stays full for one second the push fails and the producer drops and frees the message — there is no persistence or retry. Here the queue is nearly empty, so the message simply waits for the single consumer.
steps.representation:
xQueueSend(s_inbound_queue, &msg, 1000 ms)   # message_bus.c:25
  queue depth: 16 (MIMI_BUS_QUEUE_LEN)       # mimi_config.h:97
  on timeout: log 'dropping message',
              return ESP_ERR_NO_MEM
content ownership -> the queue's consumer

steps.title: Agent loop builds the prompt
steps.narrative: The agent loop task (Core 1) pops the message and rebuilds the system prompt from flash: the hard-coded preamble and tool guidance, SOUL.md, USER.md, MEMORY.md, the last three days of notes, and the skill summaries, all inside a 16 KB PSRAM buffer. A per-turn appendix adds the source channel and chat_id so tools like cron_add can target the right chat.
steps.representation:
context_build_system_prompt(buf, 16 KB)    # context_builder.c:28
  = preamble + tool guidance
  + SOUL.md + USER.md + MEMORY.md
  + last 3 days of notes + skill summaries
+ '## Current Turn Context'                  # agent_loop.c:65
    source_channel: telegram, source_chat_id: <id>

steps.title: Session history joins the turn
steps.narrative: The loop loads this chat's history from /spiffs/sessions/tg_<chat_id>.jsonl — the tg_ prefix is hard-coded for every channel — ring-buffering the last 20 stored messages into a 32 KB JSON buffer. It parses that into a cJSON messages array and appends the new user message. Only final user/assistant texts were ever stored, so no tool rounds appear in history.
steps.representation:
session_get_history_json(chat_id, buf, 32 KB, 20)
  reads tg_<chat_id>.jsonl                   # session_mgr.c:16
  ring buffer: last 20 {role, content}       # session_mgr.c:65
messages = [ ...history,
             {role: user, content: 'turn on the relay on pin 5'} ]

steps.title: Working status goes out first
steps.narrative: Before the first API call, the loop pushes a one-shot 'mimi is working...' status message to the outbound queue (skipped for system-channel turns). The outbound dispatch task pops it and routes by channel string — here to telegram_send_message — so the user sees activity while the cloud call takes its seconds. Replies and status share the same queue and dispatcher.
steps.representation:
mimi_msg_t status { channel="telegram",    # agent_loop.c:222
                     chat_id=<id>,
                     content="mimi is working..." }
  -> message_bus_push_outbound(&status)
outbound_dispatch_task:                      # mimi.c:66
  channel == telegram -> telegram_send_message()

steps.title: Cloud LLM call (blocking, whole response)
steps.narrative: llm_chat_tools serializes the system prompt, messages, and the pre-built tools JSON into one request body and performs a single blocking HTTPS POST to the configured provider — Anthropic Messages natively, or OpenAI Chat Completions through the translation layer. There is no streaming: the response accumulates in a PSRAM buffer and is parsed whole. max_tokens is 4096.
steps.representation:
POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages   # llm_proxy.c:192
  { model, max_tokens: 4096, system,          # mimi_config.h:88
    messages: [...], tools: [12 tools] }
  esp_http_client_perform()  (blocking)       # llm_proxy.c:280
  -> full JSON buffered in PSRAM, then parsed

steps.title: Model asks for gpio_write
steps.narrative: The response's stop_reason is 'tool_use' with one call: gpio_write {pin: 5, state: 1}. At most 4 calls per response are parsed. The loop appends the assistant content (text plus tool_use blocks) to the messages array, then executes each call and builds the tool_result blocks. A cron_add call would get its chat target patched to this turn's chat here; gpio_write passes through unchanged.
steps.representation:
llm_response_t { tool_use: true,           # llm_proxy.h:39
  calls[0] = { name="gpio_write",
               input={"pin":5,"state":1} } }
messages += assistant [tool_use block]
build_tool_results() executes the call       # agent_loop.c:140

steps.title: Registry dispatches, policy checks, pin flips
steps.narrative: tool_registry_execute finds gpio_write by linear name match and calls its execute function — no approval step exists anywhere in this path. The tool parses the JSON, then gpio_policy_pin_is_allowed checks pin 5 against the 21-pin allowlist (and the hard blocks: USB pins 19/20 on ESP32-S3). Allowed: the pin is configured INPUT_OUTPUT and set HIGH, and the tool returns 'Pin 5 set to HIGH' into the 8 KB tool-output buffer.
steps.representation:
tool_registry_execute("gpio_write", input)  # tool_registry.c:228
  -> gpio_policy_pin_is_allowed(5) == true    # gpio_policy.c:86
     allowlist: 1-18, 21, 38, 46              # gpio_policy.h:9
  -> gpio_set_direction(5, INPUT_OUTPUT)      # tool_gpio.c:61
     gpio_set_level(5, 1)  // pin 5 = HIGH
  -> tool_result: "Pin 5 set to HIGH"

steps.title: Second call returns the final text
steps.narrative: The loop calls llm_chat_tools again with the tool_result appended. This time the response has no tool use, so the loop keeps its text ('The relay on pin 5 is on.') as the final answer and breaks. Had the model kept calling tools, the loop would stop after 10 iterations — and, producing no final text, would fall into the generic error reply instead of explaining the limit.
steps.representation:
iteration 2: llm_chat_tools(...)             # agent_loop.c:238
  resp.tool_use == false                     # agent_loop.c:245
  final_text = strdup(resp.text)
  break   // iteration cap is 10             # mimi_config.h:78

steps.title: Session saved, reply dispatched
steps.narrative: The loop appends exactly two lines to the session file — the user's text and the final assistant text, each as a JSON object with a timestamp — then pushes the reply to the outbound queue, transferring ownership of the string. The dispatch task sends it via telegram_send_message (splitting at 4096 characters if needed) and frees the content. The agent task blocks on the inbound queue again: one consumer, ready for the next message from any channel.
steps.representation:
session_append(chat_id, "user", text)       # session_mgr.c:25
session_append(chat_id, "assistant", final)
  -> tg_<chat_id>.jsonl += 2 lines
push_outbound(reply) -> dispatch task        # mimi.c:66
  -> telegram_send_message(chat_id, content)
agent task: pop_inbound(UINT32_MAX) ...      # agent_loop.c:190
